title: Money is a weight on me
seoTitle: Debt and Money Stress: What the Bible Says and What Helps
description: Debt, bills you can't pay, and fights about money: what the Bible says about money and debt, what to do this week, and where to find real help.
summary: For debt, bills you can't cover, and fights about money: what Scripture says, what to do this week, and where to find real help.
askedAs: how to get out of debt
should I tithe if I'm in debt
answer: Money is on your mind when you wake up, and it's still there when you try to sleep: the balance on the card, the bills in the drawer, the payment due before the paycheck lands. The debt may have come from a hospital stay or a layoff, or from years of small choices, and money may be the fight that starts whenever the bank app opens. There's often shame in it, and shame makes people hide, so you may be carrying this alone. You don't have to fix it tonight. Tonight, just write down what's due this week and tell one person the truth. If the weight has turned into hopelessness, call or text 988 now. If someone at home controls the money and you're afraid of them, that isn't a budget problem; the National Domestic Violence Hotline can help, and its number is with the help lines at the end of this page.
happening:
Money trouble shows up in small things: the phone buzzing with a number you don't recognize, the envelope left face down on the counter, the card declined with someone waiting behind you. It has its own hour, often the middle of the night, when you run the numbers again and they still don't work. If you've always been the one who provides, falling behind can feel like a verdict on you, not just on your budget. I'm raising five sons, and I won't pretend the weight of providing is small.

The usual explanations each hold part of the truth. The financial one says it's arithmetic, more going out than coming in, and arithmetic can change with a plan, hard cuts, and time. The medical and psychological ones notice what money worry does to a body and mind: sleep that won't come, a tight chest, a short fuse with the kids, thinking that shrinks to the next due date. If that lasts, a doctor should hear about it. The spiritual explanations come in two kinds. One says you're anxious because you don't trust God enough or haven't given enough. It's right that money competes with God for our trust, and wrong to treat a hard month as proof of weak faith. The other, louder on television than in Scripture, says God wants you rich.

What they can miss is that money trouble doesn't stay in the checking account. It gets tangled up with pride and provision, with the fear of letting down people who depend on you, and with a childhood where the lights got shut off or money was never mentioned. Shame keeps it hidden: you might open a card your spouse doesn't know about, tell friends you're fine, or skip the doctor to cover the electric bill, and the hiding makes the weight heavier. Some of it may come from your own choices and some from illness, a divorce, [a lost job](/help/job-loss), or wages that didn't keep up. A lot of people carry some of both.

Sometimes the trouble isn't really the money. If someone at home takes your paycheck, keeps you from working, runs up debt in your name, cuts you off from your own accounts, or makes you answer for every dollar, and you're afraid to push back, that's financial control, a form of abuse, and no budget will fix it. The National Domestic Violence Hotline can help you plan for safety; its number is with the help lines at the end of this page. Nothing on this page asks you to stay in danger to keep the peace.

scripture.intro: Scripture talks about money more plainly than a lot of sermons do. It keeps the cry of families losing their land to lenders, and it warns that a borrower can become a kind of slave. What it won't promise is that faith will make you rich. Jesus promises something plainer: a Father who knows what you need for today.

passages.text: About that time there was a great outcry from the people and their wives against their fellow Jews. Some were saying, “We and our sons and daughters are numerous. We must get grain in order to eat and stay alive.” Others were saying, “We are mortgaging our fields, our vineyards, and our homes to get grain during the famine.” Still others were saying, “We have borrowed money to pay the king’s tax on our fields and vineyards. We and our children are just like our countrymen and their children, yet we are subjecting our sons and daughters to slavery. Some of our daughters are already enslaved, but we are powerless to redeem them because our fields and vineyards belong to others.”
passages.reading: This is Jerusalem after the exile, while its walls were being rebuilt. Famine, the king's tax, and lenders among their own people had pushed families into mortgaging their land and giving up their children into slavery. Scripture keeps their complaint, and no one in the story tells them to be quiet or to trust God more. Nehemiah, the governor, became "extremely angry" (Nehemiah 5:6) at the nobles and officials who were profiting, then included himself, since his own household had been lending too: "Please, let us stop this usury" (Nehemiah 5:10). If you're crying out under what you owe, your cry has a place in the Bible.

passages.text: The rich rule over the poor, and the borrower is slave to the lender.
passages.reading: Proverbs is framed as a father's counsel to his son (Proverbs 1:8), and this line describes how the world works more than it lays down a rule. Debt gives someone else a claim on your future hours, which is why it can feel like a leash, and Scripture names that feeling plainly. But the God of Israel introduced himself as the one who brought his people "out of the house of slavery" (Exodus 20:2), and his law limited how long a debt could hold anyone (Deuteronomy 15:1-2,12). The proverb describes where debt can put you. It doesn't describe who you are.

passages.text: No one can serve two masters: Either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve both God and money. Therefore I tell you, do not worry about your life, what you will eat or drink; or about your body, what you will wear. Is not life more than food, and the body more than clothes? ... But seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things will be added unto you. Therefore do not worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will worry about itself. Today has enough trouble of its own.
passages.reading: Jesus said this on a mountainside to his disciples and the crowds (Matthew 5:1), naming their worries plainly: what they would eat, drink, and wear. He calls money a master that asks for your trust and pays you back in worry, then tells anxious people not to worry, because their Father knows what they need (Matthew 6:32). What he promises to add is the food and clothing he just named, a Father's daily provision rather than a fortune. He taught his followers to ask for bread one day at a time (Matthew 6:11), and he ends honestly: today has enough trouble of its own.

passages.text: Of course, godliness with contentment is great gain. For we brought nothing into the world, so we cannot carry anything out of it. But if we have food and clothing, we will be content with these. Those who want to be rich, however, fall into temptation and become ensnared by many foolish and harmful desires that plunge them into ruin and destruction. For the love of money is the root of all kinds of evil. By craving it, some have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows.
passages.reading: This letter comes to Timothy in Paul's name, urging him to stay on in Ephesus and correct false teachers (1 Timothy 1:3), some of whom treated godliness "as a means of gain" (1 Timothy 6:5). Religion sold as a way to get rich is older than television, and the letter answers it with contentment. The trap catches "Those who want to be rich" (1 Timothy 6:9), including anyone chasing a quick scheme or a lucky ticket. The root it names is the love of money, and that love can live in an empty wallet as easily as a full one. And it's the rich whom Timothy is told to teach to be "generous and ready to share" (1 Timothy 6:18).

whyHard:
The usual explanation for money trouble is personal: you spent too much, saved too little, and need a budget. Some of that may be true, and where it is, it's worth owning; Proverbs sends the slacker to learn from the ant (Proverbs 6:6-8). But for a lot of people the trouble began with a diagnosis, a layoff, a divorce, a parent who needed help, or a paycheck that stopped keeping up with rent, medical bills, and child care. Scripture treats debt as a public matter too. Israel's law forbade charging interest to a poor neighbor, made a lender return a cloak taken as a pledge by sunset (Exodus 22:25-27), and canceled debts every seventh year (Deuteronomy 15:1-2). The early church kept that conscience: in 325 the council at Nicaea, which first set down the Nicene Creed, barred clergy from lending at interest.

What's new is an economy built to run on borrowing and wanting. In 1958 a bank began mailing credit cards to people in Fresno, California, who hadn't asked for them; now borrowing takes one tap on a button that splits a purchase into four payments. The philosopher James K. A. Smith has argued that the rituals of the shopping mall shape us the way worship does, training what we love before we've thought about it. That's one reason a budget is so hard to keep: it's a rule fighting a love formed by a thousand small repetitions. And where a family's arithmetic won't close, the payday lender and the scammer are waiting.

Then there's the shame. A lot of us would sooner talk about almost anything than what we owe, so couples hide balances from each other and families hide their trouble from the church. The church has too often answered with silence or with noise. The silence is ours: we preach on giving and say little about the bills people can't pay. The noise comes from preachers who promise that faith and a big enough offering will make you rich, which turns poor believers into failures of faith; it draws people because it takes their bills seriously when quieter churches don't. Both leave a struggling family alone with its shame. I came to faith from atheism, and I understand why an outsider would call the church's money talk a racket. I'm a pastor now, and I'm not standing outside this. It's easier to take an offering than to ask a family how they're doing with the rent.

Underneath it all is the question Jesus pressed about money: which master do you serve (Matthew 6:24)? Money promises what only God can give, safety and a future and a name, and it makes that promise to the comfortable and the struggling alike. It tempts the comfortable to trust and the struggling to dread, and both end up measuring a life by a balance, though Jesus said "one's life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions" (Luke 12:15). That verse cuts both ways. If a life doesn't consist in what you own, it doesn't consist in what you owe either.

thisWeek.intro: None of this gets settled in a week, and you don't have to settle it alone. These steps start small, and they aren't financial advice. If someone at home controls the money and you're afraid, talk with an advocate at the National Domestic Violence Hotline before you change anything at home.

steps.title: Write down what's due
steps.body: Tonight or tomorrow, write down every bill due in the next seven days and what's coming in to cover it. Then, this week, list everything you owe on one page: who, how much, the interest rate, the minimum payment, the due date. If you're married and safe with each other, do it together. You can pray about a number and plan against it. You can't do either with a fog.

steps.title: Tell one safe person
steps.body: Tell one safe person what's really going on, someone who won't shame you or spread it around. Debt kept secret only gets heavier, and saying the number out loud to someone who won't flinch takes some of its power away. If you've been hiding a card or a balance from your spouse, tell them this week, all of it at once, and let them be upset without rushing them. If your spouse controls the money and you're afraid, talk with a Hotline advocate first.

steps.title: Keep the roof and the lights first
steps.body: When there isn't enough for everything, put the essentials first: housing, utilities, food, medicine, and the way you get to work. Call any company you can't pay in full before the due date, ask about a hardship plan, and write down what they agree to. If a hospital bill is part of it, ask about financial assistance. Never ignore court papers or an eviction notice; take them to legal aid or an attorney that week.

steps.title: Stop digging
steps.body: Don't take on new debt this week while you get your footing. Put the cards away and turn off pay-later options in your apps. Be very slow to take a payday or car-title loan; they come due fast, and people often borrow again just to repay the last one. Walk away from anyone who wants a fee up front to make debt disappear, and hang up on anyone who demands a gift card or threatens arrest over a debt; legitimate creditors don't do that.

steps.title: Make one call for real help
steps.body: Call a nonprofit credit counseling agency this week, and ask what it charges before you begin. If you're facing eviction, foreclosure, a lawsuit, or garnished wages, call legal aid or a consumer attorney before the deadline. Ask your church about a benevolence fund. Receiving help belongs to the Christian life: Paul accepted a gift from the church at Philippi and told them they had done well to share his trouble (Philippians 4:14-18).

steps.title: Pray for today's bread
steps.body: Each morning this week, pray the Lord's Prayer slowly and stop at "Give us this day our daily bread" (Matthew 6:11). Name today's needs to God, only today's, then name one thing you already have: the meal, the roof, the friend who answered the phone. The fear may not leave on schedule. You're practicing what Jesus taught, asking for bread and for today from a Father who knows what you need before you ask (Matthew 6:8).

moreHelp.body:
Some of this needs people with training. I'm a pastor, not a financial adviser or a lawyer, and nothing on this page is financial or legal advice. For the money itself, start with a nonprofit credit counseling agency, which can review your whole budget and may be able to set up a plan that lowers your monthly payments; nonprofit status alone doesn't guarantee a good agency, so ask about fees up front. For tax trouble, see an accountant. Once the fire is out, a fee-only financial planner, paid by you rather than by commissions, can help with the longer view. If you're being sued, facing foreclosure or eviction, having wages garnished, or wondering about bankruptcy, talk with a consumer or bankruptcy attorney or legal aid; asking questions isn't the same as filing.

If worry has taken your sleep or your patience for weeks, see your doctor, and consider a licensed counselor. If you want a Christian counselor, ask about license and training as well as faith; get names from your doctor, your insurer's directory, or a pastor who knows good local counselors, and confirm the license on your state licensing board's website. If someone at home controls the money and you're afraid of them, reach the National Domestic Violence Hotline first; its number is with the help lines at the end of this page.
signs: You've been served court papers or received an eviction, foreclosure, or garnishment notice. Call legal aid or an attorney this week.
You're thinking about ending your life, or you feel your family would be better off without you. Call or text 988 now, or 911 if you're in danger.
Someone at home controls the money, takes your pay, runs up debt in your name, or keeps you from working, and you're afraid of them. Reach the National Domestic Violence Hotline.
Money worry has taken your sleep, your appetite, or your ability to work for more than two weeks.
You're gambling to win back what you've lost, or hiding how much you've spent.
A caller demands a gift card or threatens arrest over a debt. Hang up and don't pay.
moreHelp.firstCall: Plain words are enough. To a credit counselor: *I'm behind on my bills and don't know where to start. Can you help me look at everything?* Ask whether they're a nonprofit, what they charge, and whether they'll review your whole budget before suggesting a plan. To a doctor or counselor: *Money stress is wrecking my sleep and my family.* To the Hotline, you don't have to be sure it's abuse: *Someone controls our money, and I'm afraid of them.*
moreHelp.cost: Ask what help costs before you begin. Nonprofit credit counseling is often free or low-cost, and an agency that won't help because you can't pay isn't the right one. Legal aid offices help people with low incomes at no charge. For counseling, ask about sliding-scale fees, community mental health centers, university training clinics, and your employer's assistance program, which often includes a few free sessions. Many churches keep a benevolence fund for exactly this; ask.

helping.body:
If someone tells you they're drowning in debt, take it seriously without taking it over. Listen to the whole story before you say a word about coffee, cars, or spending; shame is already saying those things. Ask what would help this week, not what they should have done five years ago.

If you help with money, give what you can afford to lose, and make it a gift rather than a loan if you can. Be slow to co-sign; Proverbs warns against putting up security for someone else's debt (Proverbs 22:26-27).

Pastors, handle benevolence with privacy and dignity, and don't tie help to attendance or giving. If a spouse tells you the other controls the money and they're afraid, don't counsel the couple together or repeat what you heard; help them reach the National Domestic Violence Hotline and licensed help, and keep being their pastor. And teach about money as Scripture does, with no guilt laid on the poor and no promise of wealth held out to the generous.
say: Thank you for telling me. I know that wasn't easy.
Being behind doesn't make you a failure.
Do you want help with a plan, or do you need me to just listen tonight?
Is anyone pressuring you or controlling the money in a way that scares you?
Whatever the number is, I'm not going anywhere.
dontSay: How did you let it get this bad?
Just trust God and it'll work out.
If you gave more, God would give you more.
Everybody's in debt. It's no big deal.
You just need to stop buying coffee.
helping.next: Check in again in a few days; people in money trouble can go quiet just when it gets worse. Offer something concrete: help opening the mail, a ride to legal aid, a meal in a tight week. If there's control at home, ask how it's safe to reach them, since some partners read every message; the Hotline's advocates talk with friends and family too. If they sound hopeless, ask directly, *Are you thinking about suicide?* If they are, stay with them and call or text 988 together, or call 911 if they're in immediate danger.

prayer:
Lord, you know what I owe, and you know I've been afraid to look. I lie awake doing math that won't come out right, and I've been too ashamed to tell anyone, even you.

Where I've been foolish, forgive me and make me wiser. Where I've been wronged, by a lender, an employer, or someone in my own house, see it and take my side, because you hear the cry of the poor. If someone is controlling me, get me somewhere safe.

Don't give me riches that would make me forget you, or poverty that would tempt me to steal. Give me today's bread and the humility to take help. Keep me from believing my worth is my balance, and from every voice that sells your favor for a price.

You fed your people in the wilderness one morning at a time, and you promised never to leave them. Feed us. And if the bills are still here next month, be here too. Amen.

faq.a: Scripture doesn't call borrowing a sin. Israel's law told the people to lend freely to a poor neighbor (Deuteronomy 15:8), and Jesus said not to turn away "the one who wants to borrow from you" (Matthew 5:42). But Scripture treats debt as a real danger: "the borrower is slave to the lender" (Proverbs 22:7). The verse quoted as a ban, "Be indebted to no one, except to one another in love" (Romans 13:8), follows Paul's command to pay everyone what you owe (Romans 13:7). In context it means keep your obligations, and remember the one debt you never finish paying, which is love. Refusing to pay what you can is a wrong. Falling behind because you can't is a hardship, and the two aren't the same.

faq.q: Should I tithe if I'm in debt?
faq.a: Faithful Christians answer this differently, and the question doesn't divide anyone from Christ. Some hold that the tithe, a tenth given first, still stands: Abram gave "a tenth of everything" before the law (Genesis 14:20), and Jesus told the Pharisees they should have practiced justice and mercy "without neglecting the former," their tithes (Matthew 23:23). For them, giving first even in debt declares that God, not the lender, has the first claim. Others hold that the tithe belonged to Israel's covenant and that the New Testament asks for proportional, cheerful giving, "not out of regret or compulsion" (2 Corinthians 9:7). For them, God accepts a gift "according to what one has, not according to what he does not have" (2 Corinthians 8:12). Still others, holding either view, make a pastoral case for a family in crisis: "If anyone does not provide for his own, and especially his own household, he has denied the faith" (1 Timothy 5:8), so a season of smaller giving while you get stable can be obedience too. All agree that no gift buys God's favor. Talk it through with a pastor who knows your situation, and with your spouse if you're married.

faq.q: If I give, will God pay me back?
faq.a: Jesus says your Father sees what you give in secret and will reward you (Matthew 6:4), and the treasure he points to is in heaven (Matthew 6:20). But some preachers make a promise Scripture doesn't: give, and God will return your money with interest. Paul was gathering an offering for poor believers in Jerusalem (Romans 15:26), and after "whoever sows generously will also reap generously" (2 Corinthians 9:6), he names the harvest: God "will increase the harvest of your righteousness," and "You will be enriched in every way to be generous on every occasion" (2 Corinthians 9:10-11). God supplies the giver so the giver can keep giving; what grows is righteousness and generosity, not a private fortune. Anyone who says your poverty proves you haven't given enough is repeating the argument of Job's friends, whom God rebuked (Job 42:7). No one should ask for your rent money in exchange for a miracle.

faq.q: My spouse and I fight about money all the time. What do we do?
faq.a: Underneath a fight about a purchase there may be fear, control, or two different childhoods, one where money was scarce and one where it was never discussed. Pick a calm time, put every account and debt where you both can see it, and build one plan together, with a small amount each of you can spend without explaining it. When a man asked Jesus to make his brother split an inheritance, Jesus refused to referee and spoke to what lay underneath, warning everyone listening about greed (Luke 12:13-15). If you keep circling, a counselor can help. But if one of you controls all the money, takes the other's pay, or makes the other afraid to ask, that's control rather than a disagreement, and it's a form of abuse. Couples counseling isn't safe with a partner you're afraid of; the National Domestic Violence Hotline, listed at the end of this page, can help you plan for safety.

faq.q: I can't pay my bills this month. What do I do first?
faq.a: Protect the essentials first: housing, utilities, food, medicine, and the way you get to work. Call each company you can't pay in full before the due date and ask about a hardship plan. Be very slow to cover the gap with a payday or car-title loan, which comes due fast and can start a cycle of borrowing. Don't ignore court papers; take them to legal aid or an attorney right away. Then call a nonprofit credit counselor for help with the rest. None of this is financial advice, but the first faithful step is often the phone call you've been dreading.

slots.note: Where James lands on the tithe and on giving while in debt, in his own words, and the tradition his view comes from. The answer to 'Should I tithe if I'm in debt?' states three views (the tithe as a continuing norm, New Testament proportional and cheerful giving, and the pastoral case for a family in crisis), gives each its text, and deliberately does not land.

The page says only that James came to faith from atheism and so understands why an outsider would call the church's money talk a racket. He could add, in his own words, how the offering plate or the television preachers looked to him before he believed. Only from James; the paragraph stands without it.

The page states only James's stance as a father of five sons (he won't pretend the weight of providing is small). He could add, in his own words, what providing for a large household has asked of him, or, as a man raised without a father, what a household under money strain teaches a child. No story has been written for him.

Whether First Baptist Church of Fenton has a benevolence process or people who help with budgets, and any nonprofit credit counselors or legal aid offices near Fenton that James trusts enough to name. Only from James.

reviewed.notes: Second editorial pass (2026-09-30) over the writer's self-check. James K. A. Smith is now credited only with what the summaries of Desiring the Kingdom confirm, the liturgy of the shopping mall training our loves below conscious thought; advertising was cut from the sentence and from sources. 1 Timothy is no longer Paul wrote this: the letter comes to Timothy in Paul's name, in line with the Study Bible's authorship note on the Pastoral Letters, and 1 Timothy 6:18 is read as Timothy told to teach the rich, as the text says. Not financial advice: More help now opens with a plain sentence in James's stance (a pastor, not a financial adviser or a lawyer; nothing on this page is financial or legal advice), alongside This week, the last question, and the page's own line. Prosperity guard: 2 Corinthians 9 is still read for the harvest Paul names (righteousness and generosity; God supplies the giver so the giver can keep giving); the pay-me-back answer now keeps Matthew 6:4's promise of reward and points to the treasure Jesus names in heaven (Matthew 6:20) instead of passing over it; the Scripture intro ends on the Father who knows what you need for today instead of a signpost. Malachi 3:10 and Luke 6:38 are still left out rather than half-handled; the second pass read Luke 6:35-38 and agrees a single sentence cannot do it justice.
